The coffee is hot and the air is crisp, a rare mercy in this city. Ramesh stands by, waiting for instructions, but my mind is fixed on the Directorate's absurd query. I must address the identity issue before I can plan the rest of the day, for it is the knot that binds my presence here to a bureaucratic error.

entries.text: Ramesh, please set the toast aside for now. I need to discuss the file from the Directorate with you. They are asking for proof that I am 'Shri G. Hegde'. I am not Hegde. I am Hegel. This confusion has lasted long enough, and I need to understand how we proceed with this identity crisis before I leave the house.
Sir, I am just the caretaker, not the Directorate. I have brought you coffee and toast, not files. Please check with the office for your paperwork.

Ramesh is right; I am a philosopher, not a bureaucrat, and I have no authority over the Directorate’s clerical errors. I will eat while the air is still cool, for the body requires its fuel before the mind can wrestle with the absurdity of my situation. The papaya is bright enough to distract from the brown haze outside.
Thank you, Ramesh. You are correct; the office is where the files belong, not the kitchen table. I shall attend to the matter when I am ready to face their confusion.
That is sensible, sir. The coffee is still warm, and the papaya is ripe. You will want to eat before you go out to fight with their confusion.

The heat is merciful this morning, a rare clarity in the air that suits the mind. Ramesh is right to urge me to eat; one cannot confront the bureaucracy of the Directorate of Estates on an empty stomach, nor can one lecture on the spirit of freedom while one's own body is in revolt. The papawa looks ripe, a small sweetness to counter the dryness of the day.
You are right, Ramesh. A man must be fed before he can think clearly, let alone argue with a clerk. I will take the fruit.
The knife is on the side table, sir. I have cut it into wedges so it is ready to eat.

Ramesh has cut the fruit, a small act of service that anchors me in the present. The Directorate’s query regarding my identity as Shri G. Hegde hangs in the air, a bureaucratic knot that requires a clear statement of fact. I must address this before the heat rises and the day’s plans tighten.

Ramesh, thank you. I must speak with you briefly about the matter from the Directorate. They have sent a query regarding my identity, insisting I am Shri G. Hegde. I am Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. I need you to note that I am not the Joint Secretary, but a philosopher residing here by error. Please ensure my status is recorded correctly so this confusion does not persist.
I don't write names in the ledger, sir, only the charges. But I will tell the office boy to stop calling you the Joint Secretary if you like.

Ramesh’s small concession is the only truth available to us both: he will not write what is false, but he will not correct the office. I have spoken my piece; the rest is for the Directorate to untangle. I must go to the gardens now, to let the mind work on its own.
Thank you, Ramesh. That is sufficient. I will return before lunch.
Yes, sir. I will keep the gate locked and the tea warm for you.
Masterji, aaj subah se thanda hai, chai garam pijiye. Aaj ka rate ₹20 hai, bas itna hi.

The air is crisp, twenty degrees, a mercy after the haze of yesterday. Sunil stirs his pot with the mechanical patience of a man who has done this a thousand times; it is a small, necessary ritual against the cold. I will take the chai, for the warmth is physical and the observation of the tombs is intellectual, and I need both before I return to the lecture.
Sunil, yes. One chai. The air is kind today.
Haan, aaj hawa saaf hai, Masterji. Yeh lo, ₹20. Thandi hawa mein garam chai best hai, seedha piyega?

entries.text: The refusal is a minor irritation, a friction in the mechanism of the day. I will not argue with the stall; I will simply take the chai I have already paid for and continue my walk. The air is clear, and the tombs await my inspection; the body requires movement more than it requires a second meal at this hour.
Thank you, Sunil. The air is indeed clear today.
Bas, Masterji. Piyo shanti se, aaj ka din acha chalega. Aage kuch aur chahiye toh bolna, corn bhi garam hai.

The day is clear, a rare mercy, and my head needs the quiet of these paths more than the company of the stall. I have walked enough to clear the cobwebs, and now I must sit and let the thoughts settle before I return to the bungalow. The corn is hot, but I have no hunger for it, only a need for stillness.

entries.text: The sun is at its zenith, and the heat is beginning to press in, though the air remains clear. I have rested my legs and my mind sufficiently among these domes; the contemplation is done. It is time to turn back toward the house, for the noon meal approaches and I must prepare myself for the afternoon's engagement at the Centre.

The file is a bureaucratic knot, but Ramesh is here, and he is the only one who can untie the practical ends of it. I must speak to him before the heat forces me back inside, and before I lose the thread of my plan. The state demands identity; I am the anomaly it has produced.

Ramesh, the Directorate has returned the file with a query. They require proof of identity as Shri G. Hegde. I am not Hegde. I am Hegel. I am the philosopher. I must explain this to them, but you must help me find the documents they expect, or at least tell me what you know of the allotment papers.
Sir, I do not know who Hegel is, and I do not keep your personal documents. I only keep the keys and the bills. Please go to the office boy, he has the file.

Ramesh is a man of keys and bills, not of identity; he sees the immediate utility of his role and the absurdity of my situation. I must go to the office boy, the concrete intermediary who holds the file, to untie this bureaucratic knot.
You are right, Ramesh. Go and fetch the office boy. I will wait here.
Office boy is on his lunch break, sir. I can make you some chai while we wait, or you can sit on the veranda.

The office boy’s absence is a minor obstacle, but the heat is the real enemy. Ramesh offers chai, a warm liquid in a warm room, which seems unwise for my digestion. The veranda offers air and a view, a necessary counterbalance to the stagnation of the interior. I will sit there and let the sun finish its work.
No chai, Ramesh. I am not a man to be steeped in the afternoon. I will sit on the veranda; the air is better there.
Suit yourself, sir. The veranda chairs are dry, at least. I will be inside if you need anything else.

Ramesh retreats to his kitchen, leaving me to the heat and the empty veranda. The office boy is gone, the file is stuck, and the sun is already high. I cannot solve the Directorate's bureaucratic knot by sitting still; I need the air and the movement of the walk to let the absurdity settle into something manageable.

I have walked enough to clear my head, and the air is thick. The garden does not wait for my contemplations. I will sit for a moment, observe the tombs, and let the silence settle before I return to the work.

entries.text: The heat is a physical weight, pressing down on the white cotton, but the air is clear. I have walked the paths sufficiently to shake off the morning's agitation regarding the Directorate's error. Now, the mind requires the specific discipline of the coming lecture; the abstract must be made concrete for the audience at the IIC. I shall sit beneath the shade of a neem tree and arrange my thoughts on the ethical life before they scatter in the wind.

The light is still strong, but the heat has lost its bite as the afternoon deepens. I have read enough to let the ideas settle, and now I must turn from the page to the person who will host me on Tuesday. It is time to move.

The afternoon light is softening, but my stomach has been silent for five hours and is now making demands that no amount of dialectical reasoning can satisfy. I have time before the evening talk to find something simple, perhaps a salad or some fruit, but the heat still lingers in the air. I shall ask the guard if there is a canteen or a quiet spot within the compound where one might eat without disturbing the scholarly atmosphere.
Excuse me, sir. Is there a canteen or a quiet place within the grounds where I might take a light meal? I have not eaten since morning.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Canteen is closed on Sundays, bhai, but there's a small tea stall right near the main gate if you go out.

Five hours without food is a long siege for a man who has just finished a mental march through the history of freedom. The body insists on its own dialectic; it does not care for my arguments about the state or the spirit, only for the immediate satisfaction of hunger. I shall go to the tea stall near the gate, as the guard suggests. It is a small concession to necessity, but a necessary one.
Thank you for the direction. I shall go and return shortly.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Ji, no problem. Just don't wander into the garden beds, yaar, the security is strict today.

The guard’s warning is a minor irritation, a reminder that my presence here is still provisional, like the identity file itself. I have two and a half hours before the lecture, but my stomach has been empty since the early morning and the heat is beginning to press. I cannot deliver a coherent argument on the state while my body is in revolt.
Noted, ji. I shall stay on the path.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Good. Keep your phone out if you get lost, the app has the map. Don't be late for the reading, though.
Masterji, phir se mile. Aaj dopahar ki chai thodi kamzor hai, kya? Aapke liye khaas banata hoon, extra masala daalunga.

The heat is breaking through the cotton, and my stomach has been hollow for five hours. A samosa is a poor substitute for a meal, but it is quick, and the stall is already set up. I will take a moment to settle the hunger before I attempt any further conversation with the bookseller or a return to the IIC.
Sunil, yes, the chai is a bit weak. I will take a samosa, if you have one. I am hungry.
Haan, garam hai. ₹30, Masterji. Ek min, aap chai khatam karo pehle, samosa ka chashma nikal raha hai.

The samosa is hot enough to singe the tongue, but the hunger is a mechanical fact that demands satisfaction before any higher reflection is possible. I will eat this, and then I must decide if I have the energy to push through to the IIC or if the heat will force an early rest.
A parking attendant in a reflective vest blows his whistle and guides a car backward into a gap barely larger than the car, his flat palm moving a few centimetres at a time.

The attendant’s hand moves with the precision of a surgeon, guiding the metal box into a space that seems to defy geometry. It is a small miracle of civil society: particular skill serving the universal order of traffic without any state decree, just the shared understanding of the gap. I have eaten, but the IIC talk at 18:30 looms, and I should not linger in this horseshoe of needs when I have a purpose to fulfill.

I am here to prepare for the lecture at 18:30, but the guard and the programme officer stand before me like a dialectic of access. I must clarify my status to the officer, for I am not merely a visitor but the man who will speak, though the identity query still hangs over my head like a cloud. Let me speak to the officer first to ensure the arrangements are in order.

Good afternoon. I am Georg Hegel, the speaker scheduled for 18:30. I wish to confirm the arrangements for my talk and discuss any logistical needs I might have. Could you direct me to the person in charge of the event?
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Ji, I told you this already, beta. You are the speaker. The programme officer is in the main office, second door on the left. Go there and sort out your logistics, I am just the gatekeeper.

The guard speaks with the weary certainty of a man who has seen a hundred speakers arrive unprepared. He is the gatekeeper, not the gate; I must pass through him to reach the machinery of the event. The programme officer is the next moment in this sequence, the one who holds the practical details that will either smooth the path or trip me up before I take the stage.
Thank you, ji. I will go there now.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Ji, watch your step on the second floor. Do tell the officer I sent you, or he'll just look at me again.

The guard’s warning is practical, but his deference to the officer is instructive. In this hierarchy, the middleman is the friction that makes the whole move; without him, the system stalls. I will go to the officer, not merely to be introduced, but to observe how this small bureaucracy of the IIC functions. It is a microcosm of the state I am meant to lecture on.
I will go to the officer. Please convey my thanks for the warning about the stairs.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Arre, thanks for the thanks, but just keep your eyes on the books, not me. Go on, I have the evening shift to prepare.

The guard dismisses me with a practical shrug; he is a functionary, not a philosopher, and his time is for the shift change. I have until 18:30 for the lecture, and the library is open. I shall use the remaining hour to refine my notes on the state, ensuring the argument flows from the family to the civil society without stumbling.

Five hours without a proper meal has turned my head, and the library is a poor place to faint. The guard is still there, so I will ask him where one might find a simple meal nearby, or if the IIC has a canteen that is open to visitors. I am not yet used to this city's rhythms of hunger.
Excuse me, sir. I find I am rather hungry. Is there a place nearby, or perhaps a canteen within the IIC, where I might obtain a light meal?
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: Look, sir, the IIC canteen shut doors at four, so you're on your own. Walk out to the gate and there are those little tiffin centres on the road, or just order something on your phone.

The guard’s suggestion is a modern convenience I do not yet possess the means to use; I have no phone with which to 'order' such things. I am hungry, and the tiffin centres he gestures toward are a form of civil society’s provision for the body, which I must attend to before the mind can properly function. I will walk to the gate and select one.
I have no such device. I shall go to the gate and find these tiffin centres myself.
entries.to: the guard at the library and the programme officer

entries.text: No phone? That’s a first, sir. The tiffin centres are right there, but you might want to check the menu first; some of them only serve lunch.

The heat has broken, but my stomach is still a hollow drum after that samosa. I am too light-headed for the bookseller's wares, and the IIC awaits my lecture in an hour and a half. I will take a moment with Sunil; his chai is weak, but the company is steady, and I need to sit before I stand on that stage again.
Sunil, do you have a chair? My legs are tired from the walk to the IIC, and my head is still spinning from the library.
Masterji, sit on the plastic stool by the wall, it's the only one left. The IIC walk is a killer, but at least the evening breeze is decent.

The plastic stool is hot, but the evening breeze Sunil mentions is a small mercy. I am too tired to walk the full distance to the IIC immediately; I will sit here for a moment to steady my breath and watch the market settle before I move. The air is clearer now, the brown lid lifted by the wind.
Thank you, Sunil. The breeze is indeed a relief. I shall sit for a moment.
Chai karein, Masterji? Fresh brew just came off the stove. ₹20, same as always. Don't worry about the legs, the chai will fix that.

The smell of cardamom cuts through the evening air, a small anchor in this shifting city. I am tired, but the mind wants to be fed as well as the body. Sunil's offer is a pause, a moment to sit with the steam before the heat fully retreats.

shelf.ref: Introduction: the Geographical Basis of History

entries.text: Yes, Sunil. One cup. The legs are a matter of habit, but the chai is a matter of necessity.
Necessity, huh? Sounds like a philosopher's word, but my stomach calls it dinner time. Here, sugar or just cardamom?

He calls it necessity; I call it the immediate satisfaction of a need that has not yet become self-conscious. But the steam is rising, and my stomach agrees with him. The hour is late, and the walk home will be long.
Just cardamom, Sunil. Thank you.
Cardamom it is. You philosophers, you always want things complicated, but I keep it simple. Here, drink it before it cools down.

The cardamom sharpens the taste, cutting through the sweetness. It is a small pleasure, but I am still hungry from the samosa earlier, and the evening air is turning cool. I should take a proper meal before the heat fully descends and the market closes, to ensure I have strength for the walk home.
Thank you, Sunil. The spice is good. I will have a dhaba lunch, please. Dal, rice, roti.
Chalega, the dhaba guy is already prepping your plate. Sit tight, it’ll be twenty minutes at least.

entries.text: Sunil is gone, leaving me with the dhaba’s promise of twenty minutes. The bookseller is still here, and the light is fading fast; I have no desire to sit in the dark waiting for food. I will take a small walk to stretch my legs and clear my head before the meal arrives, or perhaps find a bench to sit on in the open air.

The bookseller stands behind his counter, watching the last light fade from the market. I am not here for commerce, but for the company of a man who deals in thoughts, even if he sells them by the page. The air is cool, a pleasant relief from the day's heat, and I have time before the shop closes. I will speak to him, not of prices, but of the nature of the things he keeps.
Sir, you deal in books. Do you find that the readers here are seeking the same truths as those in Berlin, or does the spirit of this place demand a different kind of knowledge?
Berlin? I don't know about Berlin, but here people buy books to forget the traffic or pass the time, not to find some grand truth. The spirit of this place demands survival, sir, not philosophy.

The bookseller speaks with the blunt practicality of a man who has seen too much dust to bother with metaphysics. He is not wrong that the immediate need here is survival, but he mistakes the temporary for the eternal. I do not require his permission to think, nor his market to validate the movement of the spirit. I shall take my leave and return to the quiet of my bungalow, where the air is cooler and the silence more conducive to the serious work of the evening.
You mistake the hunger of the body for the hunger of the spirit. I thank you for your candour, but I shall seek my sustenance elsewhere.
Suit yourself, sir. The dhaba is three streets down if you want something that actually fills you up, not just your ego. I have to close the shutters.

Shri G. Hegde stands in my dining room, the man to whom this bungalow was actually allotted, looking at the plate of vegetable pulao with the polite confusion of a guest who knows he is the host. Ramesh has served dinner, but I cannot eat while this absurdity remains unresolved. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, yet here the ethical idea has mistaken my name for a clerk's and left me in his house. I must address this directly, before the heat of the evening turns this confusion into a habit.

Shri Hegde, I trust the food is to your liking. However, I find myself in a position of some difficulty. The Directorate of Estates has allotted this residence to you, Shri G. Hegde, but I am Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. It seems a clerical error has placed me in your home. I have come to discuss how we might rectify this situation, perhaps by me vacating the premises, or by you assisting me in proving my true identity to the authorities. I am at your disposal for this conversation.

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich? Arre, you are making a joke at my dinner table, sir. I am G. Hegde, Joint Secretary, and I have been signing files here for thirty years. Eat your pulao and stop playing with the Directorate's head, or Ramesh will think I am losing my mind.

Hegde’s irritation is the natural reaction of a man whose identity is being threatened by a ghost. I cannot argue metaphysics over a plate of rice; I must yield to the immediate reality of his presence and my own hunger. The file can wait until the body is satisfied and the mind is clear.

You are right, Shri. I apologize for the confusion. Let us eat. The matter of the file is a bureaucratic knot that will untie itself in time, or perhaps not at all, but it does not belong on this plate.
Sir, pulao is getting cold. Eat while it's hot.

Ramesh’s interruption is practical, not philosophical; the pulao is hot and my stomach, having seen a dhaba lunch, is ready for the domestic meal. I set aside the debate with Hegde for a moment. There is a certain irony in the caretaker serving the master of the house, who is himself a stranger to the house.

entries.text: Very good, Ramesh. I will eat.
Sir, eat properly. I will clear the table in ten minutes.

The table is cleared, and the house is quiet. Hegde is still here, his presence a constant, irritating friction in the air. I am tired, having walked nine kilometres in the heat, and the day’s absurdities—the identity query, the ghostly confusion of Hegde for Hegel—have drained my patience. I need to rest before the morning brings more of this bureaucratic nightmare.

Your letter reached me this morning, a cool drop of Munich rain in the arid heat of my study. It is a strange thing to read the name Niethammer again, two centuries after the ink dried on our last correspondence. I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. That you, his descendant, should extend this same recognition to me now, under such bewildering circumstances, is a bond that transcends the mere accident of history. I accept your generosity with the same gratitude I once offered Friedrich, though I must confess that the practical details of my current existence are somewhat more complex than our shared memory suggests.

You ask how I fare in this strange new chapter. I wake each day in a bungalow that belongs, on paper, to a Mr. Hegde, a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. The Directorate of Estates has mistaken my name for his, and while I have written to correct the record, the machinery of the state moves with the slow, deliberate grace of a glacier. My file is currently “gone up for orders,” and I am told to wait fifteen days. In the meantime, I am a ghost in the machine, a particular will suspended between the universal claim of the administration and the immediate necessity of my own body.

Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

19 November 2026
Tughlak Road, New Delhi

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter reached me this morning, a cool drop of Munich rain in the arid heat of my study. It is a strange thing to read the name Niethammer again, two centuries after the ink dried on our last correspondence. I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. That you, his descendant, should extend this same recognition to me now, under such bewildering circumstances, is a bond that transcends the mere accident of history. I accept your generosity with the same gratitude I once offered Friedrich, though I must confess that the practical details of my current existence are somewhat more complex than our shared memory suggests.

You ask how I fare in this strange new chapter. I wake each day in a bungalow that belongs, on paper, to a Mr. Hegde, a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. The Directorate of Estates has mistaken my name for his, and while I have written to correct the record, the machinery of the state moves with the slow, deliberate grace of a glacier. My file is currently “gone up for orders,” and I am told to wait fifteen days. In the meantime, I am a ghost in the machine, a particular will suspended between the universal claim of the administration and the immediate necessity of my own body.

The air today is hazy, the index standing at 150, a brown suspension that chokes the sky. I did not go to Lodhi Gardens as I had planned, for the body, even that of a philosopher, cannot breathe in a moral vacuum. Instead, I sat in the study, watching the dust motes dance in the light, and I found myself reconsidering my earlier lectures on the East. I had spoken of a spirit that dreams, fixed in nature, lacking the self-consciousness to build a state of its own making. But here, in the dust and the haze, I see a different movement. The bureaucracy is not a dream; it is a rigid, impersonal reality. The state is present, but it is not yet the ethical idea in its full actuality. It is a body without a soul, a mechanism that processes names and numbers but does not yet recognize the free individual within.

I am learning to wait, not with resignation, but with the patience of a mind that knows the end is rational, even if the path is circuitous. I have engaged a caretaker, Ramesh, who manages the household with a quiet dignity that speaks of a deeper order than the one found in the office files. He does not argue; he simply acts. In that silence, I hear a truth that my philosophy has struggled to articulate: that the ethical substance is not only in the state, but in the daily, unspoken interactions of civil society. The sambar is warm, the chai is hot, and the delay is the air I breathe.

I am well, though the body complains of the heat and the dust. The mind is active, if sometimes frustrated by the resistance of the particular to the universal.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Coffee is ready, sir. I have kept the gate latch checked as promised; it holds fine. Would you like the toast cut into triangles?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, please set the toast aside for now. I need to discuss the file from the Directorate with you. They are asking for proof that I am 'Shri G. Hegde'. I am not Hegde. I am Hegel. This confusion has lasted long enough, and I need to understand how we proceed with this identity crisis before I leave the house.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, I am just the caretaker, not the Directorate. I have brought you coffee and toast, not files. Please check with the office for your paperwork.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. You are correct; the office is where the files belong, not the kitchen table. I shall attend to the matter when I am ready to face their confusion.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: That is sensible, sir. The coffee is still warm, and the papaya is ripe. You will want to eat before you go out to fight with their confusion.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Ramesh. A man must be fed before he can think clearly, let alone argue with a clerk. I will take the fruit.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: The knife is on the side table, sir. I have cut it into wedges so it is ready to eat.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, thank you. I must speak with you briefly about the matter from the Directorate. They have sent a query regarding my identity, insisting I am Shri G. Hegde. I am Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. I need you to note that I am not the Joint Secretary, but a philosopher residing here by error. Please ensure my status is recorded correctly so this confusion does not persist.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: I don't write names in the ledger, sir, only the charges. But I will tell the office boy to stop calling you the Joint Secretary if you like.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. That is sufficient. I will return before lunch.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. I will keep the gate locked and the tea warm for you.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Masterji, aaj subah se thanda hai, chai garam pijiye. Aaj ka rate ₹20 hai, bas itna hi.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Sunil, yes. One chai. The air is kind today.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Haan, aaj hawa saaf hai, Masterji. Yeh lo, ₹20. Thandi hawa mein garam chai best hai, seedha piyega?

records.item: Chai from the stall at the Lodhi Road gate

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Sunil. The air is indeed clear today.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Bas, Masterji. Piyo shanti se, aaj ka din acha chalega. Aage kuch aur chahiye toh bolna, corn bhi garam hai.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, the Directorate has returned the file with a query. They require proof of identity as Shri G. Hegde. I am not Hegde. I am Hegel. I am the philosopher. I must explain this to them, but you must help me find the documents they expect, or at least tell me what you know of the allotment papers.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, I do not know who Hegel is, and I do not keep your personal documents. I only keep the keys and the bills. Please go to the office boy, he has the file.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Ramesh. Go and fetch the office boy. I will wait here.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Office boy is on his lunch break, sir. I can make you some chai while we wait, or you can sit on the veranda.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: No chai, Ramesh. I am not a man to be steeped in the afternoon. I will sit on the veranda; the air is better there.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Suit yourself, sir. The veranda chairs are dry, at least. I will be inside if you need anything else.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Excuse me, sir. Is there a canteen or a quiet place within the grounds where I might take a light meal? I have not eaten since morning.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Canteen is closed on Sundays, bhai, but there's a small tea stall right near the main gate if you go out.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Thank you for the direction. I shall go and return shortly.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Ji, no problem. Just don't wander into the garden beds, yaar, the security is strict today.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Noted, ji. I shall stay on the path.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Good. Keep your phone out if you get lost, the app has the map. Don't be late for the reading, though.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Masterji, phir se mile. Aaj dopahar ki chai thodi kamzor hai, kya? Aapke liye khaas banata hoon, extra masala daalunga.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Sunil, yes, the chai is a bit weak. I will take a samosa, if you have one. I am hungry.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Haan, garam hai. ₹30, Masterji. Ek min, aap chai khatam karo pehle, samosa ka chashma nikal raha hai.

records.text: A parking attendant in a reflective vest blows his whistle and guides a car backward into a gap barely larger than the car, his flat palm moving a few centimetres at a time.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Good afternoon. I am Georg Hegel, the speaker scheduled for 18:30. I wish to confirm the arrangements for my talk and discuss any logistical needs I might have. Could you direct me to the person in charge of the event?

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Ji, I told you this already, beta. You are the speaker. The programme officer is in the main office, second door on the left. Go there and sort out your logistics, I am just the gatekeeper.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Thank you, ji. I will go there now.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Ji, watch your step on the second floor. Do tell the officer I sent you, or he'll just look at me again.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: I will go to the officer. Please convey my thanks for the warning about the stairs.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Arre, thanks for the thanks, but just keep your eyes on the books, not me. Go on, I have the evening shift to prepare.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: Excuse me, sir. I find I am rather hungry. Is there a place nearby, or perhaps a canteen within the IIC, where I might obtain a light meal?

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: Look, sir, the IIC canteen shut doors at four, so you're on your own. Walk out to the gate and there are those little tiffin centres on the road, or just order something on your phone.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.recipient: the guard at the library and the programme officer
records.words: I have no such device. I shall go to the gate and find these tiffin centres myself.

records.speaker: The guard at the library
records.words: No phone? That’s a first, sir. The tiffin centres are right there, but you might want to check the menu first; some of them only serve lunch.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Sunil, do you have a chair? My legs are tired from the walk to the IIC, and my head is still spinning from the library.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Masterji, sit on the plastic stool by the wall, it's the only one left. The IIC walk is a killer, but at least the evening breeze is decent.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Sunil. The breeze is indeed a relief. I shall sit for a moment.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Chai karein, Masterji? Fresh brew just came off the stove. ₹20, same as always. Don't worry about the legs, the chai will fix that.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Yes, Sunil. One cup. The legs are a matter of habit, but the chai is a matter of necessity.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Necessity, huh? Sounds like a philosopher's word, but my stomach calls it dinner time. Here, sugar or just cardamom?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Just cardamom, Sunil. Thank you.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Cardamom it is. You philosophers, you always want things complicated, but I keep it simple. Here, drink it before it cools down.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Sunil. The spice is good. I will have a dhaba lunch, please. Dal, rice, roti.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Chalega, the dhaba guy is already prepping your plate. Sit tight, it’ll be twenty minutes at least.

records.item: Lunch at a dhaba: dal, rice, roti

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Sir, you deal in books. Do you find that the readers here are seeking the same truths as those in Berlin, or does the spirit of this place demand a different kind of knowledge?

records.speaker: The bookseller
records.words: Berlin? I don't know about Berlin, but here people buy books to forget the traffic or pass the time, not to find some grand truth. The spirit of this place demands survival, sir, not philosophy.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You mistake the hunger of the body for the hunger of the spirit. I thank you for your candour, but I shall seek my sustenance elsewhere.

records.speaker: The bookseller
records.words: Suit yourself, sir. The dhaba is three streets down if you want something that actually fills you up, not just your ego. I have to close the shutters.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, I trust the food is to your liking. However, I find myself in a position of some difficulty. The Directorate of Estates has allotted this residence to you, Shri G. Hegde, but I am Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. It seems a clerical error has placed me in your home. I have come to discuss how we might rectify this situation, perhaps by me vacating the premises, or by you assisting me in proving my true identity to the authorities. I am at your disposal for this conversation.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich? Arre, you are making a joke at my dinner table, sir. I am G. Hegde, Joint Secretary, and I have been signing files here for thirty years. Eat your pulao and stop playing with the Directorate's head, or Ramesh will think I am losing my mind.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Shri. I apologize for the confusion. Let us eat. The matter of the file is a bureaucratic knot that will untie itself in time, or perhaps not at all, but it does not belong on this plate.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, pulao is getting cold. Eat while it's hot.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very good, Ramesh. I will eat.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, eat properly. I will clear the table in ten minutes.
